  3. Get Your Temporary Access Token:

  1. Navigate to the Webex Messaging documentation area:

docs.title: Step 1.3: Use the "Webex Messaging" Collection in Postman
docs.text:
We'll now fork the "Webex Messaging" collection into your personal Postman space, set up your authentication, and make some practical API calls.

  1. Fork the "Webex Messaging" Collection:
  2. In the Webex Public Workspace, locate the "Webex Messaging" collection in the left sidebar.
  3. Hover over the collection name and click the "..." (ellipsis) icon, then select "Fork".
  4. In the dialog box, give the Fork label a name of “Webex API Fork”.
  5. Choose your personal workspace (it should be selected by default if you're in your own workspace).
  6. Also include the “Webex Prod US1” environment in the fork (we will use this environment later).
  7. Click "Fork Collection".
  8. You should now see a copy of "Webex Messaging" in your personal workspace (usually listed under "Collections" in the left sidebar).
  9. Configure Collection Authentication and Variable:
  10. Click on your forked "Webex Messaging" collection in the left sidebar.
  11. In the main Postman window, click the "Variables" tab.
  12. Add a new variable:
  13. VARIABLE: webex_token
  14. VALUE: Paste the Bearer Token you copied from the Webex Developer Portal in Step 1.1.2 here.
  15. Now, click the "Authorization" tab for the collection.
  16. For the TYPE, select "Bearer Token".
  17. In the Token field, enter {{ webex_token }}.
  18. Explanation: This sets up the collection to automatically use your webex_token variable for all requests within it!
  19. Make Your First API Call with Postman (Get My Own Details):
  20. In your forked "Webex Messaging" collection, expand the "People" folder.
  21. Click on the GET Get My Own Details request (which corresponds to GET /v1/people/me).
  22. In the main request window, ensure the "Authorization" tab shows "Inherit auth from parent" or "Bearer Token" and that {{ access_token }} is in the Token field (if not inheriting).
  23. Click the blue "Send" button.
  24. You should receive a 200 OK response with your user details, just like in the Developer Portal.
  25. List Your Webex Spaces (Rooms):
  26. In your forked "Webex Messaging" collection, expand the "Rooms" folder.
  27. Click on the GET List Rooms request (which corresponds to GET /v1/rooms).
  28. Uncheck all the Query Params in the Params tab.
  29. Click the blue "Send" button.
  30. You should receive a 200 OK response. In the JSON body, you'll see a list of your Webex spaces. Carefully locate your personal lab space (e.g., [Your Name/ID] - API Lab Space) and copy its id value. You'll need this in the next steps!
  31. Send a Message to Your Lab Space (POST Create a Message):
  32. In your forked "Webex Messaging" collection, expand the "Messages" folder.
  33. Click on the POST Create a Message request (which corresponds to POST /v1/messages).
  34. In the main request window, click the "Body" tab.
  35. You'll see a JSON body. Remove all fields except for “roomId” and “text”.
  36. Replace {{ roomId }} with the actual id of your lab space (e.g., "roomId": "c2lkOi8v...").
  37. Change the text field to something personal, like "text": "Hello from Postman - this is much easier!".

    • Click the blue "Send" button.

  • You should receive a 200 OK response. Now, check your Webex Client – you should see the message appear in your lab space!

  • In the main request window, click the "Params" tab.
  • Uncheck all Query Params.

docs.title: 2 – Creating an Integration
docs.text:
In Chapter 1, you used a temporary developer token for quick API tests. While convenient, this isn't how real-world applications securely access user data. This chapter introduces Webex Integrations and the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow, the standard for third-party applications to get secure, user-consented access to Webex APIs. You'll create your own integration, perform a manual OAuth flow, and then configure Bruno to handle it seamlessly.

Upon completion of this section, you will be able to:

  1. Create a Webex Integration
  2. Perform a manual OAuth 2.0 authorization flow
  3. Configure OAuth 2.0 authentication in Bruno
  4. Make API requests with the obtained token in Bruno

Reference:

  • Bruno OAuth 2.0
  • Webex collection in the lab repo: bruno/Webex Messaging/

docs.title: Step 2.1: Create Your Webex Integration on the Developer Portal
docs.text:
First, you need to register your "application" (in this case, our Bruno setup) with Webex. This process gives you a Client ID and Client Secret, which are essential for the OAuth flow.

  1. Navigate to "My Apps" on the Developer Portal:
  2. Open your browser and go to https://developer.webex.com/my-apps.
  3. Ensure you are logged in with your lab credentials.
  4. Create a New Integration:
  5. Click the "Create an Integration" button.
  6. Fill in Integration Details:
  7. Integration Name: [Your Name/ID] - Lab Integration (e.g., JaneDoe-Lab Integration)
  8. Description: Webex One Lab Integration for API testing.
  9. Icon: Pick your favorite color icon.
  10. App Hub Description: "Bruno Integration for the Webex One 2026 Lab"
  11. Redirect URI(s): This is critical! For Bruno's OAuth helper, register the callback URL shown in Bruno's OAuth configuration panel when you configure collection auth (typically a localhost callback such as http://127.0.0.1:6274/callback). Confirm the exact URL in Bruno before saving your integration.
  12. Scopes: Check the following boxes:
    • spark:messages_write
    • spark:messages_read
    • spark:people_read
    • spark:rooms_read
  13. Click "Add Integration".
  14. Record Your Client ID and Client Secret:
  15. After creation, you'll see your integration's details. Copy and save your Client ID, Client Secret, and OAuth Authorization URL to a temporary text file or notepad.
  16. For best results, leave this page open for the rest of the lab.
  17. Note: The Client Secret is only shown once. If you lose it, you'll have to regenerate it.

docs.title: Step 2.2: Manual OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow (Browser + API Call)
docs.text:
Now, let's manually walk through the steps a user and an application would take to get an access token using the Authorization Code flow. This will help you understand the underlying mechanics.

  1. Use the Authorization URL:
  2. Copy the "OAuth Authorization URL" from the Integration Details page Paste this URL into your browser's address bar.
  3. Query Params Explanation:
    • response_type=code: We want an authorization code.
    • client_id: Your integration's unique ID.
    • redirect_uri: Where Webex sends the user back after authorization. Must match what you registered.
    • scope: The permissions we're requesting.
    • state: An optional parameter for security, usually a random string.
  4. Authorize the Integration (User Consent):
  5. Press Enter to navigate to the constructed URL.
  6. You'll be prompted to log in to Webex (if not already) and then asked to grant permission to your [Your Name/ID] - Lab Integration for the requested scopes.

docs.title: 2 – Creating an Integration (Postman)
docs.text:
Note

This is the legacy Postman version. For the 2026 lab, use Lab 2 - Creating an Integration with Bruno instead.

In Chapter 1, you used a temporary developer token for quick API tests. While convenient, this isn't how real-world applications securely access user data. This chapter introduces Webex Integrations and the OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow, the standard for third-party applications to get secure, user-consented access to Webex APIs. You'll create your own integration, perform a manual OAuth flow, and then configure Postman to handle it seamlessly.

Upon completion of this section, you will be able to:

  1. Create a Webex Integration
  2. Perform a manual OAuth 2.0 authorization flow
  3. Configure OAuth 2.0 authentication in Postman
  4. Make API requests with the obtained token in Postman

docs.title: Step 2.1: Create Your Webex Integration on the Developer Portal
docs.text:
First, you need to register your "application" (in this case, our Postman setup) with Webex. This process gives you a Client ID and Client Secret, which are essential for the OAuth flow.

  1. Navigate to "My Apps" on the Developer Portal:
  2. Open your browser and go to https://developer.webex.com/my-apps.
  3. Ensure you are logged in with your lab credentials.
  4. Create a New Integration:
  5. Click the "Create an Integration" button.
  6. Fill in Integration Details:
  7. Integration Name: [Your Name/ID] - Lab Integration (e.g., JaneDoe-Lab Integration)
  8. Description: Webex One Lab Integration for API testing.
  9. Icon: Pick your favorite color icon.
  10. App Hub Description: “Postman Integration for the Webex One 2026 Lab”
  11. Redirect URI(s): This is critical! For Postman's built-in OAuth helper, we'll use a specific callback URL. Enter: https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback
  12. Scopes: These define what permissions your integration will request from the user. Check the following boxes:
  13. spark:messages_write
  14. spark:messages_read
  15. spark:people_read
  16. spark:rooms_read
  17. Click "Add Integration".
  18. Record Your Client ID and Client Secret:
  19. After creation, you'll see your integration's details. Copy and save your Client ID and Client Secret and OAuth Authorization URL to a temporary text file or notepad. These are sensitive credentials and will be needed shortly.
  20. For best results, leave this page open for the rest of the lab.
  21. Note: The Client Secret is only shown once. If you lose it, you'll have to regenerate it.

docs.title: Step 2.2: Manual OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow (Browser + API Call)
docs.text:
Now, let's manually walk through the steps a user and an application would take to get an access token using the Authorization Code flow. This will help you understand the underlying mechanics.

  1. Use the Authorization URL:
  2. Copy the “OAuth Authorization URL” from the Integration Details page Paste this URL into your browser's address bar:
  3. Query Params Explanation:
  4. response_type=code: We want an authorization code.
  5. client_id: Your integration's unique ID.
  6. redirect_uri: Where Webex sends the user back after authorization. Must match what you registered.
  7. scope: The permissions we're requesting.
  8. state: An optional parameter for security, usually a random string.?
  9. Authorize the Integration (User Consent):
  10. Press Enter to navigate to the constructed URL.
  11. You'll be prompted to log in to Webex (if not already) and then asked to grant permission to your [Your Name/ID] - Lab Integration for the requested scopes.
  12. Uncheck the “Only ask when requesting new permissions.” checkbox. This way, when we authorize again later, we will see the same dialog.
  13. Click "Accept"
  14. Capture the Authorization Code:
  15. Webex will redirect your browser to https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback?code=YOUR_AUTHORIZATION_CODE&state=set_by_app.
  16. Copy the authorization code value from the URL in your browser's address bar. This is your temporary authorization code.
  17. Exchange the Code for an Access Token (Postman API Call):
  18. Open Postman.
  19. Create a new HTTP Request (click the + tab).
  20. If it doesn’t say “HTTP”, you will need to change the type.
  21. Set the request method type to POST.
  22. Set the URL to: https://webexapis.com/v1/access_token
  23. Go to the "Body" tab, select x-www-form-urlencoded.
  24. Add the following key-value pairs:
    • Grant Type
    • KEY: grant_type
    • VALUE: authorization_code
    • Client ID
    • KEY: client_id
    • VALUE: YOUR_CLIENT_ID (Paste your Client ID)
    • Client Secret
    • KEY: client_secret
    • VALUE: YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET (Paste your Client Secret)
    • Auth Code
    • KEY: code
    • VALUE: YOUR_AUTHORIZATION_CODE (Paste the code you captured in step 3)
    • Redirect
    • KEY: redirect_uri
    • VALUE: https://oauth.pstmn.io/v1/callback
  25. Click "Send".
  26. Observe the Token Response:
  27. You should receive a 200 OK response containing your access_token, refresh_token, expires_in (how long the access token is valid), and scope.
  28. Copy your new access_token. This token was generated via your integration and user consent, making it a more secure way to access Webex APIs on behalf of a user.
  29. Update Postman Collection with New Token:
  30. In your personal Postman workspace, navigate to your forked "Webex Messaging" collection.
  31. Click on the collection name in the left sidebar, then select the "Variables" tab in the main window.
  32. Find the webex_token variable you created in Chapter 1.
  33. Paste the webex_token you just copied from step 5 into the " Value" column for webex_token.
  34. Make an API Call with the Integration Token (List Rooms):
  35. In your forked "Webex Messaging" collection, expand the "Rooms" folder.
  36. Click on the GET List Rooms request (which corresponds to GET /v1/rooms).
  37. Click the blue "Send" button.
  38. You should receive a 200 OK response. Verify that the rooms listed are correct for your lab account. This call was made using the access_token obtained through your integration!

docs.title: Receiving events in real time
docs.text:
Webex bots can receive events in two main ways:

  • Webhooks: Webex sends HTTP callbacks to a public URL. This works well in production, but usually requires a public endpoint or a tunnel such as ngrok during development.
  • WebSockets (Mercury): Your bot opens a persistent connection to Webex and receives events in real time. This works well in lab environments and corporate networks because no public URL is required.

In this lab, your bot connects to Webex Mercury. You will implement event handling, message parsing, and Adaptive Card actions directly in Python.

"""Validate Agentic App credentials and Webex connectivity."""

import os
import sys

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

APP_ID = os.getenv("AGENTIC_APP_ID")
APP_TOKEN = os.getenv("AGENTIC_APP_TOKEN")
BASE_URL = os.getenv("AGENTIC_APP_BASE_URL", "https://webexapis.com/v1")
SPACE_ID = os.getenv("LAB_SPACE_ID")


def check_env() -> None:
    missing = [name for name in ("AGENTIC_APP_ID", "AGENTIC_APP_TOKEN") if not os.getenv(name)]
    if missing:
        print(f"Missing required variables: {', '.join(missing)}")
        sys.exit(1)
    print(f"Agentic App ID configured: {APP_ID}")


def check_webex_token() -> None:
    response = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/people/me",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {APP_TOKEN}"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    profile = response.json()
    print(f"Authenticated as: {profile.get('displayName')} ({profile.get('emails', [''])[0]})")


def check_space_access() -> None:
    if not SPACE_ID:
        print("LAB_SPACE_ID not set; skipping space check.")
        return
    response = requests.get(
        f"{BASE_URL}/rooms/{SPACE_ID}",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {APP_TOKEN}"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    room = response.json()
    print(f"Space accessible: {room.get('title')}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    check_env()
    check_webex_token()
    check_space_access()
    print("Agentic App configuration looks good.")

python 01_configure_agent.py

docs.text:
Goal: Perform common Webex tasks through MCP instead of direct API calls.

  • [ ] Use an MCP tool to retrieve user or room information
  • [ ] Use an MCP tool to send a message or create a space
  • [ ] Use an MCP tool to perform one admin or automation action relevant to the lab

Sample prompts to try in your MCP client:

Send a message to room ROOM_ID saying: "Hello from the Webex MCP lab!"

Equivalent direct API call for comparison (08-mcp/01_list_rooms.py):

"""Compare MCP tool usage with a direct Webex REST call."""

import os

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

TOKEN = os.getenv("WEBEX_ACCESS_TOKEN")
response = requests.get(
    "https://webexapis.com/v1/rooms",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
    timeout=30,
)
response.raise_for_status()

for room in response.json().get("items", []):
    print(f"{room['title']} ({room['id']})")
